papers.title: A live online exercise program for older adults improves depression and life-space mobility: A mixed-methods pilot randomized controlled trial
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2024, Multidisciplinary; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The primary aim was to determine the preliminary effectiveness of a live online exercise program from qualified instructors on older adults’ PA levels compared to a waitlist control group. The paper notes that older adults have described numerous barriers to participating in PA and exercise.
papers.methodology: Pilot convergent parallel mixed-methods randomized controlled trial comparing a live online exercise program (ACTIVE) with a waitlist control (CON). Community-dwelling older women and men between the ages of 65 and 80 were recruited in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada, through newsletters, social media and a local newspaper, between November 2020 and November 2021. Measures included an armband BodyMedia Sensewear Pro II accelerometer and questionnaires administered online using LimeSurvey; qualitative interviews were semi-structured and audio recorded via Zoom. Analysis used a two-way repeated measures ANOVA and thematic analysis in Dedoose.
papers.theory: The design was guided by the CONSORT 2010 statement (extension for pilot and feasibility trials); no theory is named.
papers.results: On the Geriatric Depression Scale there was an interaction (p = 0.012), with the ACTIVE group decreasing from pre-to-post intervention. For life-space mobility there was an interaction (p = 0.014), with the ACTIVE group increasing. There were no differences between groups for daily steps and daily active energy expenditure, and no significant between or within-group differences for symptoms of anxiety and loneliness. Attendance was 97% in the ACTIVE group, and participants were satisfied or very satisfied 98% of the time.
papers.discussion: The authors report that the program did not affect habitual PA levels but reduced depressive symptoms, improved life-space mobility, and had excellent adherence and acceptability. They describe online exercise programs as viable service-delivery options, particularly when in-person programming is unavailable, and recommend future work on synchronous online resources to engage older adults in exercise.
papers.limitations: The authors acknowledge the small sample size; the pilot was underpowered to determine if there was an interaction for the primary outcome. They also note a lack of blinding of assessors and participants to group allocation, and that only English-speaking individuals with internet access at home were included. Future studies should attempt to include marginalized populations, and future work will focus on the effectiveness of group-based synchronous exercise programs on functional assessments.

Following the intervention, participants in the ACTIVE group reported reduced symptoms of depression (ACTIVE: pre = 4.2 ± 2.5; post = 2.2 ± 1.9; CON: pre = 3.5 ± 2.1, post = 3.5 ± 2.1; p <0.001) and improved life-space mobility (ACTIVE: pre = 62.4 ± 14.7; post = 71.8 ± 16.0; CON: pre = 65.1 ± 19.0, post = 63.6 ± 22.0; p = 0.003) compared to waitlist control participants.
The ACTIVE group had good adherence (97%) and acceptability (98%).

Five themes were identified, including (1) Feasibility of the online exercise program; (2) Perceived health benefits and improvements; (3) Registered Kinesiologists and Physiotherapists contributed to perceived safety; (4) Social connectivity associated with synchronous/live delivery; and (5) Growing old gracefully and preventing disability.
Our online exercise program was acceptable to older adults, had good adherence, reduced depression, and increased life space.
Participants reported improved functional and mental health benefits.
Further research is warranted to expand on these findings.

papers.title: Effectiveness of exercise-based rehabilitation for depressive symptoms, anxiety, and health-related quality of life in adults with rheumatoid arthritis: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Multidisciplinary; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The review aimed to evaluate the effects of structured exercise on depressive symptoms, anxiety and HRQoL in adults with rheumatoid arthritis, and, where data allowed, whether effects differed between conventional and mind-body exercise. The authors state that whether exercise improves these outcomes remains uncertain.
papers.methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing structured exercise with non-exercise control conditions, in adults aged 18 years or older with RA. PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and EBSCOhost were searched from inception to November 26, 2025, and two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts. Random-effects meta-analyses in RevMan 5.4 used Hedges’ g; risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE.
papers.theory: The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement; no theory is named as guiding the review.
papers.results: Depressive symptoms (11 trials, 685 participants): SMD = −0.49; 95% CI, −0.70 to −0.28; P < 0.001; I² = 42%. Anxiety (7 trials, 403 participants): SMD = −0.45; 95% CI, −0.65 to −0.25; P < 0.001; I² = 0%. Quality of life (7 trials, 564 participants): SMD = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.18 to 0.71; P = 0.001; I² = 50%. No statistically significant subgroup difference between conventional and mind-body exercise was observed for these outcomes. Certainty was rated moderate for depressive symptoms and low for anxiety and HRQoL.
papers.discussion: The authors conclude that structured exercise was associated with reductions in depressive symptoms and anxiety and with improvements in HRQoL, and that exercise may provide psychological and quality-of-life benefits as an adjunct to standard RA care. They state that current evidence is insufficient to identify the most effective exercise modality, dose, supervision strategy, or delivery format, and that exercise should not be viewed as a substitute for pharmacologic disease control or formal mental-health care when these are indicated.
papers.limitations: The authors note that the included trials were generally small and varied in intervention characteristics, comparator conditions, and outcome instruments, and that most psychological and HRQoL outcomes were self-reported with participant blinding usually infeasible. Few studies per outcome limited subgroup precision and the assessment of publication bias. Most analyses used immediate post-intervention outcomes, so durability remains uncertain. The review included only English-language full-text articles, which the authors say may have introduced language bias.

abstract_claims.q: Although exercise is recommended as part of comprehensive care, its effects on psychological outcomes and quality of life remain uncertain.

Compared with non-exercise controls, structured exercise reduced depressive symptoms (11 trials, 685 participants; standardized mean difference, −0.49; 95% confidence interval, −0.70 to −0.28; P < 0.001; I² = 42%; moderate certainty).

Low-certainty evidence suggested reductions in anxiety (7 trials, 403 participants; standardized mean difference, −0.45; 95% confidence interval, −0.65 to −0.25; P < 0.001; I² = 0%) and improvements in quality of life or health-related quality of life (7 trials, 564 participants; Hedges’ g standardized mean difference, 0.45; 95% confidence interval, 0.18 to 0.71; P = 0.001; I² = 50%).
Subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant difference between conventional exercise and mind-body exercise.

Structured exercise probably reduces depressive symptoms and may reduce anxiety and improve quality of life in adults with rheumatoid arthritis, supporting its use as an adjunct to comprehensive care.
Larger, better-reported trials with longer follow-up are needed to clarify durability, clinical importance, and optimal delivery.

papers.title: Effectiveness of aerobic physical exercise on depression symptoms in adults: A protocol for developing a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Multidisciplinary; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The protocol aims to guide a future systematic review of the effects of aerobic exercise on reducing depression levels in adults. The paper notes that, although the benefits of aerobic exercise for depressive symptoms are well documented, the existing literature shows high variability in modality, intensity, frequency and duration.
papers.methodology: Protocol for a systematic review with meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials. The population is adults with depression, the intervention is aerobic exercise, and the comparator is other types of exercise, placebo or control. The databases BVS, Cochrane library, Embase, Epistemonikos, PubMed and SPORTDiscus will be searched using MeSH and EMTREE descriptors, with no restriction on date or language. Two reviewers will select studies using Rayyan; quality will be assessed with TESTEX and RoB 2.0, and certainty with GRADE.
papers.theory: The protocol follows the guidelines developed by Page et al. (PRISMA-P); no theory is named.
papers.results: The paper is a protocol and reports no results.
papers.discussion: The authors expect the review to identify the effective dose-response for reducing depression levels and to provide an understanding of the mechanisms through which aerobic exercise influences depression. They describe aerobic exercise as a potential strategy for treating depression, and suggest it has great potential to be integrated into therapeutic strategies, especially for patients who do not fully respond to conventional treatments.
papers.limitations: The authors anticipate limitations and challenges: small sample sizes, lack of clarity about the mechanisms through which exercise improves depression, variations in the intensity protocols adopted, and high heterogeneity among the studies to be included. They say the review aims to highlight these issues.

papers.title: Physical activity and depressive symptoms among college students: positive mental health as a mediator
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Psychology (miscellaneous); not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The study aimed to explore whether positive mental health mediates the relationship between physical activity and depressive symptoms. The authors note that the psychological mechanisms of physical activity remain a key issue, as traditional explanations have mostly focused on direct relief of negative emotions and stress.
papers.methodology: A cross-sectional study using a convenience sample of Chinese college students, collected through the Wenjuanxing online survey platform between May and June 2025. The final sample comprised 3,140 participants from 22 provinces in China. Measures were the PARS-3, the Positive Mental Health Scale and the PHQ-9. Analyses used Spearman’s rank correlation and mediation analysis with PROCESS macro (version 4.1), using a bias-corrected bootstrap with 5,000 resamples, in SPSS 29 and AMOS 29.
papers.theory: The study is anchored in Self-Determination Theory, which identifies autonomy, competence and relatedness as three innate psychological needs.
papers.results: Physical activity showed a small but significant positive link to positive mental health (ρ = 0.143) and a weaker negative connection to depressive symptoms (ρ = −0.089). The direct effect was non-significant (c’ = −0.008, p = 0.080), and the indirect effect through positive mental health was significant (ab = −0.007, 95% CI [−0.010, −0.004]). The model explained little variance (R2 = 0.014 for positive mental health).
papers.discussion: The authors describe a small indirect association consistent with a mediation pattern, in which positive mental health may function as a mediator. They propose positive mental health as a useful conceptual focus for future research. They propose a multi-tiered strategy for colleges, including spaces, facilities and sports programs, mental health education courses, and physical activity prescriptions within personalized care plans for students needing support.
papers.limitations: The authors state that the cross-sectional design prevents confirmation of causal sequences, and that the convenience sampling frame limits the generalizability of the results. They note that the internal consistency of the PARS-3 scale was modest (α = 0.634). They propose longitudinal studies using experience sampling methods, replication in more diverse, probabilistically sampled populations, and cross-cultural validation.

papers.title: A Pilot Cross-Sectional Study on the Level of Depression and Physical Activity among Students in Poland and Portugal in the Second Year of the COVID-19 Pandemic
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2023, Medicine (miscellaneous); not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The study aimed to make a preliminary assessment of depression rates and physical activity levels, and the relationship between them, among Polish and Portuguese students in the further year of the COVID-19 pandemic. The authors note that restrictions on exercise have largely led to a decline in daily physical activity.
papers.methodology: An online cross-sectional survey of students from Poland and Portugal, conducted in October 2022 with a Google form shared through e-learning platforms and Facebook private groups. The analysed sample was 398 students (229 from Poland, 169 from Portugal), aged 17 to 26. Depression was measured with the Beck Depression Inventory and physical activity with an abbreviated International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ). Analyses used Mann–Whitney, chi-square, Spearman’s rank correlation and Kruskal–Wallis tests in Statistica v. 13.
papers.results: Moderate depression affected 20–35% of respondents, and depression was generally lower among men. There were no differences between countries in the distribution of depression classifications. Portuguese women showed a different activity profile, with fewer in the low-activity group (16% vs. 34%). In both countries, more frequent walking had the strongest effect on reducing depression (Poland rS = −0.42; Portugal rS = −0.28).
papers.discussion: The authors report that depression severity tended to decrease with more physical activity, and that a subgroup analysis showed physical activity at a certain intensity could reduce students’ depressiveness. They describe the prevalence of depression among these students as alarming and conclude that further research on physical activity and mental health is needed to adjust the optimal level of activity.
papers.limitations: The authors state that the cross-sectional nature of the study does not provide robust and causal evidence, that the small sample and preliminary findings are limitations, and that self-report questionnaires may bias responses. They also note that social media may distort the data and affect the representativeness of the sample. They propose future studies with a larger sample and more objective methods to assess the parameters studied.

papers.title: Experiences of exercise and mental well-being among psychiatric inpatients: a qualitative study
papers.introduction: The study aimed to explore psychiatric inpatients’ experiences of exercise and its perceived impact on mental well-being during hospitalization. The authors note that research on exercise among psychiatric inpatients remains limited, and that less is known about how these patients experience exercise.
papers.methodology: A qualitative study with a purposive sample of eight inpatients (five male, three female; mean age 53.9) at the University Hospital of North Norway, who had taken part in individualized exercise sessions with an exercise physiologist. Participants were recruited by an exercise physiologist and took part in a telephone interview, using a semi-structured guide with open-ended questions. Interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim. Data were analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis.
papers.theory: The analysis took a contextualist perspective.
papers.results: Four themes were identified: follow-up support, symptom reduction, sense of mastery, and activation during hospitalization. Support from the exercise physiologists was highlighted as a crucial factor for initiating and maintaining exercise. Many described how exercise instantly helped reduce anxiety, anger, and depressive symptoms. The perceived effects were not uniformly strong, and some participants were uncertain about effects on sleep or energy.
papers.discussion: The authors suggest that adequate support and follow-up are key to implementing physical exercise interventions for inpatients in psychiatric care, and that more inpatients should be given the opportunity to participate in regular physical exercise. They state that the findings reflect participants’ subjective experiences and should not be interpreted as evidence of treatment efficacy or causal effects of exercise. They describe physical activity as a supplement to established interventions rather than a replacement for them.
papers.limitations: The authors note that the sample of eight participants is relatively small, and that a possible selection bias may exist because those who chose to participate may have been more positively inclined toward exercise. They state that the single-center Norwegian setting may limit transferability, that the study had no comparator, and that telephone interviews limited access to non-verbal cues. They call for future research with a broader and more diverse sample, including psychiatric inpatients specifically, and for further research to examine efficacy and identify active components of the exercise intervention.

papers.title: Improvements in physical activity and depression symptoms: an observational study of users of a multi-modal digital mental health platform
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2025, Biomedical Engineering; 3 other categories also Q1; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The study aimed to analyze depression and physical activity among employees seeking support from a digital mental health platform, examine their baseline association, and investigate changes over time. The authors note a paucity of data on the impact of a multi-modal digital mental health platform like this on different areas of health and well-being.
papers.methodology: Prospective, observational study of adults with access to an employer-sponsored, multi-modal digital mental health benefits platform (Modern Health, San Francisco, CA). Conducted September 2021 to May 2022 in the United States. Participants completed an online baseline survey and a follow-up survey three months later, using the IPAQ-Short Form and the PHQ-9 on Qualtrics. Analyses were run in R, with paired t-tests and Spearman rank correlations.
papers.results: Of 755 adults at baseline, 47.3% (n = 357) were underactive. Men averaged 49 more MVPA minutes per week than women. Underactive participants (n = 211) increased MVPA by 60.33 min/week (117%), and 27.5% became active. Among those with a positive screen (n = 178), PHQ-9 fell by 4.88 points, and 66.9% improved or recovered. Active participants reported no statistically significant change in activity.
papers.discussion: The authors state that digital mental health platforms can support both symptom improvement and maintenance of positive mental health outcomes, and that digital, remotely delivered interventions may be particularly beneficial for underactive adults. They suggest that employer-sponsored platforms offering integrated mental and physical health resources may create a more supportive environment for sustaining health behaviors. They conclude there is a need for digital health platforms to broaden their focus beyond single domains.
papers.limitations: The authors state that the observational design cannot establish the temporal sequence of changes, and that an experimental design is needed to test causality. They note that the single-item impact measure has yet to be validated, that industry sector and implementation factors were not examined, and that completers were more often White, which limits generalizability. Future studies should use an experimental design and longer follow-up of 6 or 12 months.

papers.title: Chronic exercise effects on overall depression severity and distinct depressive symptoms in older adults: A protocol of a systematic and meta-analytic review
papers.quartile: Q1 (SJR 2024, Multidisciplinary; not in Psychiatry and Mental Health)
papers.introduction: The review aims to investigate the effects of chronic exercise on overall depression severity and on different symptoms of depression in older adults, in randomized controlled trials, including the moderating effects of intervention and individual characteristics. The authors state that, to their knowledge, no published review or meta-analysis has examined the broadest possible range of symptoms.
papers.methodology: Protocol for a systematic and meta-analytical review of randomized controlled trials of chronic exercise in older adults, following PRISMA-P. Eligible studies are RCTs with parallel-group or cluster designs and a mean age of 60 years or above. Several databases will be searched from inception. Two independent reviewers will conduct study selection, data extraction and quality assessment. A random-effects model will be used, with Hedges' g as the effect size, and GRADE and RoB2 will assess quality.
papers.results: The paper is a protocol and reports no results.
papers.discussion: The authors expect a moderate effect of exercise on depression compared with active and passive control groups, and expect the results to be moderated by intervention and individual characteristics. They state that the conclusions may serve as a basis for evidence-based recommendations for individualized exercise programs. They also suggest that the review results may reveal research gaps for further RCTs.
papers.limitations: The authors note that, because RCTs with pharmacological or psychotherapy effects are excluded, no conclusions can be drawn for exercise as add-on treatment, and that they may miss some clinically relevant insights. They anticipate heterogeneous data and wide variance in how exercise and individual characteristics are reported. They suggest the review may show whether comorbidities or physical fitness level still require further research.

introduction.q: the objective of the proposed review is to investigate the effects of chronic exercise on overall depression severity and on different symptoms of depression in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) including older adults with a mean age of at least 60 years
and by considering the moderating effects of intervention characteristics and individual characteristics
to our knowledge, there is no published review or meta-analysis that attempts to uncover the effects of chronic exercise on the broadest possible range of symptoms as described in the DSM

methodology.q: In this article, we have outlined a protocol for a systematic and meta-analytical review
follows the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocol (PRISMA-P) statement
Eligible studies only include RCTs with either a parallel-group design
the mean age of each arm of the RCT is 60 years or above
Our review further aims to encompass all populations of older adults independent of disease
The intervention must last at least one week and include more than one exercise session.

The following electronic databases will be searched from inception to shortly before publishing the meta-analysis: Web of Science (all bases); Academic Search Complete, MEDLINE with full text, CINAHL with full text, APA Psycinfo, SPORTDiscuss with full text through EBSCO host; Cochrane.

methodology.q: Two independent reviewers will conduct the study selection, data extraction, and quality assessment.
a random-effects model will be used for the meta-analysis
Summary effects will be calculated as Hedges’ g using random-effects weights.
The two reviewers will independently rate the quality of the included studies with ROB2.

results.q: In this article, we have outlined a protocol for a systematic and meta-analytical review on the effects of chronic exercise on depression in older adults
This protocol has been published in the Prospero repository

discussion.q: we expect to find a moderate effect of exercise on depression compared to active and passive control groups with no exercise components
We further expect the results to be moderated by intervention characteristics and individual characteristics
the conclusions drawn from this review may serve as a basis for developing evidence-based recommendations for individualized exercise programs that can help alleviate depression in older adults
the review results may reveal research gaps that can stimulate the formulation of research questions for further RCTs

limitations.q: We plan to exclude RCTs with tested effects of pharmacological treatment and / or psychotherapy.
Therefore, no conclusions can be drawn for exercise interventions as add-on treatment.
We are aware that by that we might miss some clinically relevant insights.
We further anticipate limitations in form of heterogenous data and a wide variance in the reporting of the exercise characteristics (e.g., detailedness) and the individual characteristics.
For instance, it can reveal whether certain moderator variables, such as comorbidities or physical fitness level still require further research to understand their influence.

abstract_claims.q: There is high evidence that chronic exercise benefits overall depression severity in older adults.
The results of the proposed review are anticipated to have a substantial impact on research and clinical practice.
On the one hand, the review’s conclusions could form the foundation for developing evidence-based recommendations for individualized exercise programs that alleviate depression in older adults.
by revealing research gaps, the review results could encourage the formulation of research questions for further RCTs.

caveats.q: However, the heterogeneity of the effects is high, which might be caused by variations between exercise interventions.
This might lead to methodological issues in the choice of the control group that might influence the results
For example, an RCT including an active control group with social interactions to examine the effect of an individual-based exercise intervention (without social interaction) is not appropriate.

Although in exercise interventions, these techniques are applied to the context of exercise behavior, it is plausible that they can also be translated to other areas of life, such as dealing with depression.
Meaningful responses may be only visible when the exercises are conducted with a certain frequency and duration
Nevertheless, one single score provides only limited information on the severity of the specific symptoms
These precautions might imply that the impact of exercise is insufficient for reducing depression.
Although these connections have not been investigated yet, they hold significance in the context of geriatric depression.
Although there are quite many RCTs examining the effects of chronic exercise on specific symptoms of depression
The results show, on the one hand, a high degree of heterogeneity for the exercise characteristics and, on the other hand, partly different results for the individual characteristics.
In a recent umbrella review on the effects of chronic exercise on depression in older adults, only one of the twelve included reviews was considered to be of high methodological quality
Since publication bias is seldom calculated, further evidence is needed to strengthen the evidence.
Furthermore, we will only include studies in which frequency of exercise sessions, duration of exercise sessions, duration of the intervention and type of exercise are reported.
Intervention arms comprising a chronic exercise component additionally to other intervention components, such as nutrition, cognitive behavioral therapy, or pharmacotherapy, are not eligible.
Eligible studies only include RCTs with either a parallel-group design
Abstracts from congresses and study protocols are not considered.
We plan to exclude RCTs with tested effects of pharmacological treatment and / or psychotherapy.
Therefore, no conclusions can be drawn for exercise interventions as add-on treatment.
We are aware that by that we might miss some clinically relevant insights.
We further anticipate limitations in form of heterogenous data and a wide variance in the reporting of the exercise characteristics (e.g., detailedness) and the individual characteristics.
We aim to deal with those limitations by being cautious in interpreting the results.
